entities.name: Michael IX Palaiologos
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Michael IX Palaiologos, crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire in 1294, served alongside his father Andronikos II Palaiologos until his own death in 1320. His reign, though shared, was predominantly characterized by a relentless and often desperate struggle to defend the diminishing imperial territories against a multitude of external threats, including the ascendant Ottoman Turks in Anatolia and the rapacious Catalan Grand Company in the Balkans. Michael IX was not merely a ceremonial figure; he was an active military commander who personally led imperial forces, embodying the empire's last significant efforts to stem the tide of its decline, even as its resources dwindled.

Throughout his co-rule, Michael IX was at the forefront of the Byzantine military efforts. He led campaigns against the Ottomans in Asia Minor, suffering a significant defeat at the Battle of Magnesia in 1302 against the Catalan Grand Company, which had initially been hired as mercenaries but turned against the empire. He also contended with Bulgarian incursions and internal administrative challenges, tirelessly attempting to organize defenses despite the empire's chronic lack of funds and manpower. His strategic acumen was often hampered by the empire's severe financial constraints, forcing reliance on unreliable mercenary forces and ultimately contributing to the loss of vital territories.
